title: Easy Kitchen Helpers for Stiff or Arthritic Hands
subtitle: Jar openers, reachers and easy-grip utensils that take the twist and squeeze out of everyday chores.
excerpt: Stubborn jars and high shelves don't have to win. Here are four simple tools, from a push-button jar opener to a 32-inch reacher, that ask less of sore hands.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A pickle jar that won't budge. A dropped pill bottle that rolled under the table. A faucet handle that seems tighter every winter. For many of us, the hard part of the kitchen is not the cooking. It is the gripping, twisting and pinching that comes before it.

You are far from alone. Occupational therapists writing for the National Council on Aging point to federal survey data showing that arthritis affects nearly half of Americans 65 and older. The good news is that a handful of inexpensive tools can take a lot of the twist and squeeze out of everyday chores.
"Arthritis is a reality for almost half (47.3%) of U.S. adults who are 65 and older." (National Council on Aging)
Why the right tool makes a difference

The NCOA article, written by two occupational therapists at Michigan Medicine, suggests letting bigger, stronger joints like the wrist and elbow do more of the work and avoiding hard, forceful gripping or repeated pinching. Tools with longer handles give you more leverage. Handles with a wider, non-slip surface mean your fingers don't have to clamp down as tightly.

The Arthritis Foundation makes a similar point in its list of arthritis-friendly kitchen tools. For example, it notes that pots with two handles let you spread the weight between both hands instead of straining one wrist.
What to look for before you buy

items: Fat, cushioned handles. A thicker handle is easier to hold than a thin one, and you can also slide foam tubing over tools you already own.
Longer handles or levers, which turn a small push into a bigger force.
Non-slip surfaces on the handle and, for jar openers, something that keeps the jar from spinning.
One-handed or push-button operation if both hands are stiff.
Light weight. A tool that is hard to lift is hard to use.
Easy cleaning. Check whether it is dishwasher safe, and if it runs on batteries, what kind.

sections.content: Here are four tools from different corners of the house, with prices as published by the seller in October 2026. Prices change often, so check before you order. We have not tested these ourselves; the details below come from the product listings.
Jar openers: electric or under the cabinet

There are two main approaches. A battery-powered opener like the RoboTwist sits on top of the jar and does the twisting when you press a button. Its seller lists a lid range of 1 to 3.5 inches across and notes it needs AA batteries, so keep a few on hand. An under-cabinet opener such as the EZ Off has no motor at all. It mounts beneath a cabinet with adhesive or screws, and you press the lid into its toothed grip and turn the jar. Because the opener is fixed in place, you only need to hold the jar. One caution from the listing's own reviews: the teeth can leave marks on metal lids.

A reacher, also called a grabber, saves your hands and your back. The Vive model is 32 inches long, has a claw that rotates 90 degrees, and is rated to hold up to 5 pounds, according to the maker. That covers a box of crackers on a high shelf or a dropped set of keys, but not a heavy pot.

Built-up handles help at mealtime, too. The Good Grips utensil kit sold by MaxiAids has 1-3/8-inch handles, and the fork and spoons can be bent to an angle that suits your wrist, for left- or right-handed use. If you only want one piece, ask whether the seller offers them individually.

sections.label: Good to Know
sections.content: If hand pain or stiffness is making daily tasks harder, ask your doctor for a referral to an occupational therapist or certified hand therapist. The NCOA article recommends this kind of referral for help with grip and thumb exercises, and a therapist can suggest tools that fit your hands and your home.

Not every fix needs a purchase. The NCOA suggestions include sitting while you prep, taking a break before your hands get tired, keeping everyday items on the counter or a low shelf, and sliding a heavy pot across the stove on a hot pad instead of lifting it. Pre-cut vegetables and lighter pans help as well.
Start with the chore that frustrates you most, whether that is the jar, the high shelf or the soup spoon. One well-chosen tool can make the kitchen feel like your own again.

products.name: RoboTwist Electric Jar Opener
products.blurb: A push-button, battery-powered opener that sits on the jar and twists the lid for you. The listing gives a lid range of 1 to 3.5 inches and notes it needs AA batteries.

products.name: EZ Off Under Cabinet Jar Opener
products.blurb: A manual opener that mounts under a cabinet with included adhesive or screws, so you only need to hold and turn the jar. The maker pitches it for weak hands and limited grip.

products.name: Rotating Reacher Grabber (32-inch)
products.blurb: A lightweight aluminum reacher with a 4-inch rubber-coated claw that rotates 90 degrees. The maker says it holds items up to 5 pounds.

products.name: Good Grips Utensils Sample Kit
products.blurb: A fork, small spoon, teaspoon, tablespoon and rocker knife with 1-3/8-inch built-up handles. The forks and spoons bend to any angle, and all pieces are listed as dishwasher safe.
